title: The Grand Aurora Hotel
question: How do independent hotels share a platform without sharing authority?
story: A hotel SaaS platform has a control plane, a shared production cell, and a dedicated enterprise account. Tenant discovery chooses a destination; the destination still has to authorize the guest.
prompt: Design a fictional multi-tenant hotel SaaS on AWS with control-plane, pooled-production, dedicated-enterprise and security accounts. Show staff federation, tenant discovery, pooled versus siloed data planes, scoped cross-account provisioning and central audit. Keep network, database replication and authorization details in the two companion views. Distinguish credential, request and provisioning arrows.
notes: Scope: deployment overview. Cell services and Aurora clusters are aggregates, not single-AZ instances. The companion views expand identity/isolation and one pooled cell’s availability/recovery design. They are authored views, not automatic projections.

Assumptions: tenant onboarding writes an authoritative tenant-to-cell directory; discovery returns an endpoint to the browser. Each cell independently verifies identity, tenant assignment and membership. Discovery is not a trusted authorization shortcut.

The enterprise account has separate credentials, application resources and database. Pooled isolation additionally needs transaction-local validated tenant context, a non-owner database role, forced row-level policies and tests for bypass paths.

Provisioning uses an allowlisted cross-account role and CloudFormation. Organization-trail coverage, central bucket policy, KMS permissions and retention must be configured; API audit capture is not application-log capture. No deployed configuration is supplied.

title: Hermes’ Delivery Office
question: Which tenant is allowed to publish, consume and replay each message?
story: Hermes serves two customer accounts. Standard deliveries use a shared worker cell across two AZs; an enterprise customer gets a separate account, queue, worker and ledger.
prompt: Design a fictional cross-account messaging SaaS. Bind authenticated publisher accounts to tenants; never trust a tenant ID in event detail. Show operator authentication, tenant-route administration, a pooled SQS worker cell with Fargate consumers in two private AZ placements, and a dedicated delivery account with its own bus, queue, Lambda, ledger and DLQ. Keep SQS and DynamoDB regional, outside AZ boxes.
notes: Tenant A and B are illustrative customers. Workload roles sign PutEvents; resource policies and an account-to-tenant allowlist constrain ingress and routing. Multi-tenant publishers within a single customer account would need a separately validated ingress contract.

AZ A/B contain private Fargate tasks, not independent SQS or DynamoDB instances. Assumed SQS interface endpoints have ENIs in enabled AZs; DynamoDB uses a gateway endpoint. Endpoint and security-group configuration is not drawn.

Cross-account bus forwarding requires a sender role, destination bus policy and explicit target permissions. Dedicated workers have no intended pooled-state access. These policies are design requirements, not validated IAM documents.

Queue arrows denote polling and configured redrive. Consumers need idempotency, tenant-scoped state access and a privileged, audited replay process. A shared queue is a noisy-neighbour trade-off; stricter service tiers may need more queue partitions. Recipient transport and autoscaling policies are omitted.

title: Saturday Night Queue
question: Can a flash sale survive retries without selling the same capacity twice?
story: The club has a protected edge, authenticated buyers, an authoritative sales region, asynchronous consumers and a regional recovery copy. A second region is not a second ticket counter.
prompt: Design a fictional flash-sale ticketing platform with CloudFront/WAF, Cognito, JWT API, transactional reservation and outbox, stream-driven independent consumers, separate audit account and asynchronous read-only recovery replica. Show one authoritative writer region; do not claim globally consistent active-active inventory.
notes: Reservation code must atomically enforce capacity, purchase idempotency and outbox insertion. Hold expiry is application logic; asynchronous DynamoDB TTL deletion is not a booking clock.
The Streams-to-bus element aggregates an EventBridge Pipe and its configured target. Consumers tolerate duplicate events, lag and version changes. The mail worker and connection details are omitted.

The illustrated global-table replica is read-only by application/IAM policy, not an inherently read-only DynamoDB service mode. Failover needs fencing of the old writer, reconciliation and an explicit sales-resumption decision.

CloudFront/WAF are global account resources; Cognito, SQS and DynamoDB are regional. Edge login arrows show browser identity progression. The audit arrow summarizes a separately configured pipeline, not Lambda writing directly across accounts without permission.

title: Moonshot Mission Control
question: Who can ingest telemetry, query research data and change the audit record?
story: A mission ingestion account protects the live path. A research account owns the historical lake and its key. A security account owns the audit trail.
prompt: Design a fictional modern multi-account telemetry platform. Include device certificate authentication, scoped IoT rules, Kinesis, independent live alarms and buffered archival delivery, cross-account S3/KMS permissions, federated research access and protected central auditing. This is not historical Apollo or safety-critical flight control.
notes: Device certificates and topic policies identify publishers. Consumers need timestamps, schema checks and event IDs; neither stream partitioning nor a diagram establishes global event order.

Cross-account Firehose delivery needs an execution role, destination bucket policy and KMS permissions. Research access uses scoped roles, approved datasets, workgroups and protected query-result storage; not all these resources are expanded.

Protected audit retention assumes S3 versioning, configured Object Lock and appropriately restricted administrators. The organization trail captures applicable AWS API activity, not every sensor payload.

Cognito represents federated application sign-in; a backend credential broker or approved federation path must map researchers to scoped AWS query roles. No Cognito-to-Athena direct API call is implied by the identity line. This system is fictional and has no flight-control authority.

title: The Coral Reef Observatory
question: How does an experimental model become a controlled production tool?
story: Training and production live in different accounts. A promoted model can suggest a label; authenticated reviewers decide whether the record becomes accepted evidence.
prompt: Design a fictional private ML review platform with separate research and production accounts, versioned artifacts, human-approved model promotion, private inference access, a review service across two AZs, authenticated reviewers and a workflow-gated accepted catalogue. Distinguish deployment control from inference and approval requests.
notes: Promotion assumes a reviewed artifact version, scoped cross-account deployment role and explicit bucket/key permissions. The diagram does not demonstrate model quality, safety or scientific validity.

SageMaker is shown as a regional managed service. Private inference access requires appropriate VPC endpoints and IAM/network configuration; training/inference infrastructure is not placed inside the review app’s AZ boxes.

The internal ALB is reachable only through assumed corporate/private connectivity. App-level identity verification and reviewer authorization remain necessary. Task-token callbacks go through an authenticated backend.

Only the successful approval branch publishes accepted records. Training data, predictions and accepted evidence have different retention/access policies. Training pipelines, endpoint HA settings, staff connectivity and complete audit infrastructure are omitted.

title: Midnight at the Diner
question: Can stores reconnect and replay stock updates without counting them twice?
story: Store integrations arrive from a separate account. The inventory platform reconciles a versioned journal, can place work in either AZ, and waits for a supervisor before releasing a supplier proposal.
prompt: Design a fictional multi-location inventory platform with authenticated cross-account store connectors, idempotent offline replay, a versioned stock journal, scheduled orchestration, private multi-AZ task capacity, transactional stock storage, authenticated supplier approval, failure notifications and a separate backup account.
notes: Store connectors sign API requests. Identity-to-store bindings, event IDs and monotonic source versions must be checked server-side; a store ID in JSON is not authority.

Fargate placements in AZ A/B are alternative execution capacity, not permission to execute each stock mutation twice. Reconciliation uses transactional checkpoints and bounded retries. Journal-read paths and VPC endpoints are omitted.
The supervisor callback releases a workflow approval step. Supplier ordering and payment are outside the view. Catch paths carry execution/checkpoint identifiers for recovery.

The Aurora icon is an aggregate cluster, not a single-instance HA claim. Cross-account backup needs supported resources, organization configuration, copy roles, KMS permissions, retention and tested restoration.

title: The Last Train Home
question: What must a station do after losing its region and every open connection?
story: The operational feed has its own account. Passenger regions maintain local projections and broadcasters. Reconnection includes authentication and a snapshot, not just a new socket.
prompt: Design a fictional multi-region passenger-information service with an authorized cross-account feed, ordered ingestion, version-aware primary projection, asynchronous regional replica, independent regional broadcasters/WebSocket APIs, station identity and explicit snapshot recovery. Never imply that an existing WebSocket moves between regions or that this controls trains.
notes: The operational event version is authoritative. The primary reducer rejects stale versions and duplicate events. A replicated passenger projection is not the source timetable and must not become a competing authoritative writer.

DynamoDB replication is asynchronous. Regional broadcasters consume their local streams and use local connection registries. The assumed compatible global-table/stream configuration and regional resource policies require deployment validation.

Stations reauthenticate, fetch current state plus a version watermark, then reconcile deltas after reconnect. A WebSocket CONNECT authorizer and snapshot backend enforce identity; neither is fully expanded.

The secondary snapshot endpoint, regional connection registries, routing/health checks and source-feed disaster recovery are omitted. The shown primary snapshot path alone is not a complete regional failover implementation. Passenger information only: no signalling or train control.

title: The Mixtape Archive
question: Who can upload a master, process it, and make a recording public?
story: Ingestion, processing, publication and recovery each have a different account. A successful transcode is still unpublished until the release gate approves it.
prompt: Design a fictional cross-account original-music platform with artist identity, a tenant-scoped temporary upload capability, quarantine, controlled MediaConvert jobs, unpublished renditions, human rights/release approval, a private published origin with signed CloudFront playback, and versioned cross-region master replication.
notes: The upload broker derives allowed tenant/object keys from verified identity and issues bounded temporary capabilities. The browser uploads; the identity arrow does not mean Lambda streams the audio.

Cross-account workflow and MediaConvert roles need explicit source, destination and KMS policies. Job completion and human rights approval are separate preconditions; neither S3 presence nor successful encoding grants publication authority.

Publication copies approved objects and updates the catalogue with reconciliation for partial failures. CloudFront origin access control authorizes private origin reads; signed viewer URLs separately authorize listeners.

Master replication assumes source/destination versioning, replication roles, KMS grants and deliberate delete-marker/retention policies. It is asynchronous and is not a substitute for protected backups. No real music or rights claims are made.

title: Grand Aurora: Tenant Isolation
question: Why is a valid login token insufficient to access another hotel’s records?
story: One issuer, two application accounts, and independent authorization at each cell. The pooled path binds a validated tenant to a transaction; the dedicated path also checks its cell allowlist.
prompt: Expand Grand Aurora identity/isolation. Show staff login, shared Cognito issuer, separate JWT APIs and same-account VPC Links/internal ALBs, private application membership checks, pooled Aurora row policies, and separate enterprise data. Do not assume that discovery, a JWT alone, or a client tenant header authorizes record access.
notes: Identity lines show browser-carried credentials, not Cognito initiating calls into the APIs. Each API validates issuer, audience, expiry and scopes. VPC Link integrations and internal ALBs remain in their own account/region.

The app derives the subject from verified identity, checks selected-hotel membership and assigned-cell policy, and sets tenant context locally within a transaction. A client-supplied tenant ID is a selection, not evidence of entitlement.

Pooled PostgreSQL isolation assumes non-owner/non-BYPASSRLS roles, forced row policies, safe transaction pooling and tests covering raw SQL, background workers and administrative paths. The picture does not prove those controls.

Separate enterprise credentials/database/account reduce shared-data-plane exposure; the app still rejects other tenants. Identity federation, revocation, privileged operations and complete networking are not implementation artifacts here. This is a focused authored view of the overview’s cell aggregates.

title: Grand Aurora: Failure & Recovery
question: Which failures do replicas, standby regions and backups actually cover?
story: Application replicas cover task/AZ failures. Aurora readers can become writers. A secondary region can lag. A separately controlled backup serves a different recovery purpose.
prompt: Expand one Grand Aurora pooled cell. Show regional ALB, private tasks and Aurora writer/reader in two AZ/subnet placements, shared distributed Aurora storage, reader-promotion transition, asynchronous Global Database secondary, standby app activation and isolated cross-account backups. Distinguish request, replication and recovery arrows. Do not invent RTO/RPO or active-active booking writes.
notes: AZ A/B are illustrative, not deployable AZ identifiers. ALB nodes require enabled subnet mappings in both AZs; its subnet mappings and VPC Link ingress are aggregated. Task and DB security groups need explicit rules.

Aurora compute instances use DB subnets; the shared cluster volume is regional managed infrastructure with storage across three AZs. A reader is not a separately writable replica. The recovery arrow denotes role promotion, not reverse replication.

Aurora Global Database requires supported versions/regions and asynchronously replicates storage. Standby activation requires fencing the previous writer, database promotion and traffic/credential changes. Lag, loss and manual recovery decisions remain possible.

Backups assume a supported encrypted cross-account copy configuration, dedicated roles, KMS grants and restore tests. A backup is not a hot replica. No RTO/RPO, zero-loss failover or production readiness is claimed. This view expands one pooled cell, not every enterprise deployment.
